newsitem.title: USA: NHL-RED WINGS TAKE 2-0 SERIES LEAD WITH TRIPLE OT WIN.
newsitem.headline: NHL-RED WINGS TAKE 2-0 SERIES LEAD WITH TRIPLE OT WIN.

text.p: The Russian connection came through big time for the Red Wings Sunday as Detroit grabbed a 2-0 lead in the best-of-seven Western Conference semifinals with a triple overtime victory.
Vyacheslav Kozlov took a pass from Vladimir Konstantinov and scored a powerplay goal 91 seconds into the sixth period to give the Red Wings their second consecutive overtime win.
"We put the Russians together and they got most of the shots for us," said Detroit coach Scotty Bowman, whose team unleashed 71 shots at the Anaheim net.
Anaheim defenceman J.J. Daigneault drew a penalty 63 seconds into the third overtime for hooking Doug Brown to break up a semi-breakaway.
Just 28 seconds later, Konstantinov found Kozlov, who fired a slap shot from the right faceoff circle that cleanly beat goaltender Mikhail Shtalenkov, ending the marathon.
"Our team can feel it now. We want to get to the finals," said Detroit captain Steve Yzerman.
Shtalenkov came on at 7:02 of the third period after Guy Hebert was injured lunging to stop a shot by Brendan Shanahan. Shtalenkov and Hebert combined for 68 saves for the Ducks.
Mike Vernon made 49 saves for Detroit, which played its longest game since a 5-4 triple-overtime loss to Toronto in the 1960 NHL semifinals.

"We're not at all disappointed. In fact, we're encouraged that they couldn't beat us in regulation," said Ducks coach Ron Wilson. "We were very tired in the second overtime. It's just too bad we had to kill a penalty in the third overtime and didn't get it done."

The Red Wings brought a 1-0 lead into the third period on a first-period goal by Yzerman. But veteran Jari Kurri tied it at 4:18 of the third, wristing a shot past Vernon for his 106th career playoff goal.
Detroit regained the lead just under eight minutes later when Doug Brown deflected Shanahan's cross-ice feed past Shtalenkov to make it 2-1.
Anaheim star Teemu Selanne sent the game to overtime with 3:07 left in regulation, poking in a rebound after Vernon stopped Steve Rucchin's deflection of a Dmitri Mironov shot.
Daigneault nearly won it for Anaheim in the second overtime period, but his wrist shot from the slot hit the left goalpost.

At New Jersey, Mike Richter posted his eighth career playoff shutout and Brian Leetch scored a powerplay goal in the first period as the New York Rangers posted a 2-0 victory over the Devils to even their Eastern Conference semifinal series at one game apiece.

Richter made 32 saves, including a sprawling highlight film stop on John MacLean's point-blank attempt to tie the game with just over a minute left. Russ Courtnall scored an empty net goal in the final minute to seal the victory.
The game was mirror image of Game One in which New Jersey goaltender Martin Brodeur recorded a shutout and the Devils got a powerplay goal from a defenceman and an empty netter in the final minute.
"Well, it certainly seems to be a goaltender's series -- 2-0, 2-0," observed Rangers coach Colin Campbell.

The Rangers special teams work was superb as they killed off seven Devils powerplays, including a four-minute kill late in the second period and a 5-on-3 advantage that lasted for 70 seconds in the third.

New Jersey had outshot the Rangers 16-2 when Leetch scored New York's first goal of the series with 1:39 left in the first period. Wayne Gretzky passed the puck from behind the net to Leetch, who one-timed a shot past Brodeur, ending Brodeur's playoff shutout streak at 138 minutes, 21 seconds.
"Wayne went behind the net and everybody lost me," Leetch said of the key goal.

New Jersey appeared to tie the game with 4:30 remaining in the second when Steve Thomas deflected MacLean's centering feed past Richter, but replays showed Thomas's right skate was in the crease and the goal was disallowed.

The score was still 1-0 when MacLean broke in alone and got off a backhander that looked like it would tie the game. But Richter made a sensational diving save, and while on his back swept a loose puck out of harm's way with his bare hand.
"That was the save of the game, obviously," Campbell said.
Brodeur paid tribute to his New York counterpart.
"Mike Richter...was tremendosus and he was the difference. He is so good, I have no margin to make a mistake."
